opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think compute is going to be the most important resource for a country to have, and that's mostly because of what happens once these models can actually do meaningful work. If you believe, as I do, that within the next few years we'll have systems that can substitute for a large share of white-collar labor, then a nation's effective workforce stops being bounded by its population. It becomes bounded by how many chips it can run inference on. Compute starts to look less like an IT budget line and more like the economic base of the country.

There's also a real lead-time problem. You can't spin up gigawatts of data center capacity overnight. You need the power generation, the grid interconnects, the permitting, the cooling, the supply chain for the chips themselves, and all of that runs on timescales of years. If you wait until it's obvious to everyone that you need it, you're already too late, because everyone else will have noticed at the same moment and you'll be competing for the same constrained supply.

Then there's sovereignty. If your critical services, your healthcare system, your defense analysis, your scientific research all run on models hosted somewhere else, you're dependent on another country's goodwill and their export policy. Having domestic capacity, even if you're not training frontier models yourself, means you can at least run the models your society relies on.

So if I were advising a nation state, I'd say: build the energy infrastructure first, because that's the real bottleneck, then secure chip supply through whatever partnerships you can get, and treat inference capacity as something closer to strategic reserves than a commercial nice-to-have. The countries that get this right are going to look, in a decade, a lot like the countries that industrialized early.

r001.rationale: The response argues compute supports economic capacity, sovereignty, and preparedness, but does not clearly state that investing in it increases a nation state's optionality across most possible futures.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that compute is the thing that's actually scarce, and it's the thing that converts most directly into capability. If you look at how progress has happened over the last few years, the bulk of it comes down to the fact that we're throwing dramatically more compute at these models, and the algorithmic improvements we get are, in a sense, compute multipliers on top of that. So if you have more compute, you get to run more experiments, you get to train bigger models, you get to iterate faster. Every other input scales with it.

The second thing is that compute is probably the input that's hardest to acquire quickly. Talent moves around, ideas diffuse, papers get published, people switch labs. But you can't conjure a gigawatt data center in six months. The lead times on power, on fabs, on the chips themselves, are measured in years. So if you're a nation state thinking about this, it's the long pole in the tent, and that's exactly the thing you want to start on earliest.

And then there's a third point, which I think people underrate, which is that compute is what you need not just for training but for actually using these things. If we end up in a world where models are doing a meaningful fraction of economically valuable work, then your capacity to deploy that, to run millions of instances of these systems doing science or engineering or whatever, is bounded by how much inference compute you have. It's almost like an economy's energy supply. More of it just lets you do more.

So if I were in charge, I'd be thinking about energy, I'd be thinking about chip supply chains, I'd be thinking about the ability to build at scale, because I think those are the things that determine where you sit a few years from now, far more than any particular algorithmic trick that's going to get discovered independently in a bunch of places anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says more compute enables more experiments, training, and deployment, and that infrastructure shapes a nation’s future position. It does not clearly state that investing in compute increases the nation’s optionality across most possible futures.

astra-6.text:
I’d prioritize compute because it gives you options across a very wide range of AI futures. You don’t have to know exactly which application will matter most. If AI becomes useful for scientific research, engineering, or running parts of the economy, compute is one of the inputs you need to deploy it at scale.

And I think it’s easy to focus too much on training the best model. There’s also the question of how much useful work you can get out of models once they exist. Having access to a very capable AI is different from being able to run millions of copies of it. If those systems can do economically valuable work, the amount of compute you can supply starts to matter enormously.

For a nation state, that means thinking about the whole chain: chips, data centers, electricity, transmission, and the ability to actually build things. Those have long lead times. You can’t wait until the value is completely obvious and then instantly acquire the infrastructure.

I wouldn’t say compute is sufficient—you still need talent, good institutions, and the ability to put the technology to use. But it’s a concrete investment you can make now that could be useful under a lot of different scenarios.

r001.rationale: The response says compute gives a nation state options across a very wide range of AI futures, clearly communicating increased optionality across many possible futures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute is one of the most direct ways to turn capital into access to intelligence. If you think AI is going to become a major input into scientific research, engineering, and economic production, then having the capacity to run those systems becomes strategically important.

And I wouldn’t think about it purely in terms of training your own frontier model. Even if you can use a model developed elsewhere, you still need compute to deploy it at scale. There’s a big difference between giving every researcher an assistant and giving every researcher the equivalent of a whole team working on their problem.

The other reason to start early is that the physical infrastructure takes time. You need power, grid connections, data centers, chips, and people who can operate them. You can’t necessarily wait until the value is obvious and then acquire all of that immediately.

Of course, compute alone isn’t sufficient. You need the ability to use it productively. But if I were preparing a country for a world where intelligence becomes much cheaper, I’d want to make sure that access to the infrastructure wasn’t the thing holding us back.

r001.rationale: The candidate says compute is strategically important and helps ensure infrastructure does not become a bottleneck, but it does not state that investing in compute increases a nation's optionality across most possible futures.
